theorem.content:
[Existence and Uniqueness of Fast Pulses]\label{thm: E}
When $0<\epsilon \ll 1,$ there exists a unique $C^2$ (modulo translation) fast traveling pulse solution $(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ to system \eqref{eq: intro_system_1}-\eqref{eq: intro_system_2}. In particular, with $z=x+ct$, there exists unique $C^1$ curves $c_\epsilon=c(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon=a(\epsilon)$ such that $U_\epsilon(z)<\theta$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(a_\epsilon,\infty)$ and $U_\epsilon(z)>\theta$ on $(0,a_\epsilon)$. The parameters satisfy $c_\epsilon\to c_f$ and $a_\epsilon\to +\infty$ as $\epsilon \to 0$, where $c_f>0$ is the unique speed of the front solution to \eqref{eq: intro_scalar}. As a homoclinic orbit, $\mathcal{S}_\epsilon=\Bigl\{(U_\epsilon(z),Q_\epsilon(z)): z\in \R \Bigr\}$ satisfies $d_H(\mathcal{S}_\epsilon,\mathcal{S}_0)\to 0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$. Here, 
$$
d_H(\mathcal{S}_\epsilon,\mathcal{S}_0)=\max\left\lbrace \sup_{(U,Q)\in \mathcal{S}_0}d\Bigl(\mathcal{S}_\epsilon,(U,Q)\Bigr),\sup_{(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)\in \mathcal{S}_\epsilon}d\Bigl((U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon),\mathcal{S}_0\Bigr) \right\rbrace
$$ 
is the Hausdorff distance between sets in $(U,Q)$ space with respect to the standard Euclidean metric, and $\mathcal{S}_0$ is the singular homoclinic orbit at $\epsilon=0$.
theorem.label: thm: E

sketch:
To prove \cref{thm: E}, the introduction indicates that the paper (unlike prior heuristic/computational work) provides a complete proof by \emph{deriving “a number of new estimates of the solutions and their wave speeds and widths.”} It emphasizes that, for $\epsilon>0$, \emph{“the fast and slow dynamics need to be analyzed when they overlap”} (in contrast to the singular homoclinic orbit at $\epsilon=0$), and that the approach \emph{“avoid[s] requiring”} a PDE reduction available for exponential-type kernels.

A key structural element of the argument is to characterize the pulse parameters via the \emph{“speed index equations”} for the pulse, namely $f(\tau(\epsilon),c(\epsilon),\epsilon)=U(0)=\theta$ and $g(\tau(\epsilon),c(\epsilon),\epsilon)=U(a(\epsilon))=\theta$, after introducing the rescaled width $\tau(\epsilon):=\epsilon a(\epsilon)$ as a \emph{“natural change of variable”} (since $a(\epsilon)$ is tied to fast/slow time scales). The corollary then summarizes the resulting first-order parameter information: $\tau(\epsilon)\to\tau_0$ and $c(\epsilon)\to c_f$, and $(\tau'(0),c'(0))^T$ is obtained from an implicit-differentiation/Jacobian formula $-J^{-1}(\tau_0,c_f,0)(f_\epsilon(\tau_0,c_f,0),g_\epsilon(\tau_0,c_f,0))^T$, yielding first-order approximations $\tau(\epsilon)\approx \tau_0+\tau'(0)\epsilon$ and $c(\epsilon)\approx c_f+c'(0)\epsilon$ (with an explicit expression for $c'(0)$ in \eqref{eq: cp_zero}).

mcq.question:
Let $0<\epsilon\ll1$ and consider the system
\[
 u_t=-u-q+\int_{\mathbb R}K(x-y)H\bigl(u(y,t)-\theta\bigr)\,dy,\qquad
 q_t=\epsilon\,(u-\gamma q).
\]
Under these assumptions, what is the strongest statement asserting existence together with uniqueness of a fast traveling pulse solution (including the associated traveling-wave parameters and the $\epsilon\to0$ limit behavior)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
For $0<\epsilon\ll1$, there exists a unique $C^2$ (modulo translation) fast traveling pulse solution $(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ of the system. In particular, writing the traveling-wave variable as $z=x+ct$, there exist unique $C^1$ curves $c_\epsilon=c(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon=a(\epsilon)$ such that $U_\epsilon(z)<\theta$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(a_\epsilon,\infty)$ and $U_\epsilon(z)>\theta$ on $(0,a_\epsilon)$. Moreover, as $\epsilon\to0$, one has $c_\epsilon\to c_f$ and $a_\epsilon\to+\infty$, where $c_f>0$ is the unique speed of the front solution to the corresponding scalar equation. If $\mathcal S_\epsilon=\{(U_\epsilon(z),Q_\epsilon(z)):\, z\in\mathbb R\}$ denotes the associated homoclinic orbit, then $d_H(\mathcal S_\epsilon,\mathcal S_0)\to0$ as $\epsilon\to0$, where $\mathcal S_0$ is the singular homoclinic orbit at $\epsilon=0$ and
\[
 d_H(\mathcal S_\epsilon,\mathcal S_0)=\max\left\{\sup_{(U,Q)\in\mathcal S_0} d\bigl(\mathcal S_\epsilon,(U,Q)\bigr),\ \sup_{(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)\in\mathcal S_\epsilon} d\bigl((U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon),\mathcal S_0\bigr)\right\}
\]
with $d$ the standard Euclidean distance in $(U,Q)$-space.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For $0<\epsilon\ll1$, there exists a unique $C^2$ (modulo translation) fast traveling pulse solution $(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ of the system. In particular, writing $z=x+ct$, there exist unique $C^1$ curves $c_\epsilon=c(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon=a(\epsilon)$ such that $U_\epsilon(z)<\theta$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(a_\epsilon,\infty)$ and $U_\epsilon(z)>\theta$ on $(0,a_\epsilon)$. Moreover, as $\epsilon\to0$, one has $c_\epsilon\to c_f$ and $a_\epsilon\to a_0<\infty$, where $c_f>0$ is the unique speed of the front solution to the corresponding scalar equation. If $\mathcal S_\epsilon=\{(U_\epsilon(z),Q_\epsilon(z)):\, z\in\mathbb R\}$ denotes the associated homoclinic orbit, then $d_H(\mathcal S_\epsilon,\mathcal S_0)\to0$ as $\epsilon\to0$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For $0<\epsilon\ll1$, there exists a $C^2$ fast traveling pulse solution $(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ of the system, unique up to translation. Writing $z=x+ct$, there exist (possibly nonunique) $C^1$ functions $c_\epsilon=c(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon=a(\epsilon)$ such that $U_\epsilon(z)<\theta$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(a_\epsilon,\infty)$ and $U_\epsilon(z)>\theta$ on $(0,a_\epsilon)$, and as $\epsilon\to0$ one has $c_\epsilon\to c_f$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For $0<\epsilon\ll1$, there exists a unique $C^2$ (modulo translation) fast traveling pulse solution $(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ of the system. In particular, in traveling-wave coordinates $z=x+ct$, there exist unique $C^1$ curves $c_\epsilon=c(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon=a(\epsilon)$ such that $U_\epsilon(z)<\theta$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(a_\epsilon,\infty)$ and $U_\epsilon(z)>\theta$ on $(0,a_\epsilon)$. Moreover, as $\epsilon\to0$, one has $c_\epsilon=c_f+O(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon\to+\infty$. If $\mathcal S_\epsilon=\{(U_\epsilon(z),Q_\epsilon(z)):\, z\in\mathbb R\}$ denotes the associated homoclinic orbit, then there is a constant $C>0$, independent of $\epsilon$, such that $d_H(\mathcal S_\epsilon,\mathcal S_0)\le C\epsilon$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For $0<\epsilon\ll1$, there exists a unique $C^2$ (modulo translation) fast traveling pulse solution $(U_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon)$ of the system. In particular, writing the traveling-wave variable as $z=x+ct$, there exist unique $C^1$ curves $c_\epsilon=c(\epsilon)$ and $a_\epsilon=a(\epsilon)$ such that $U_\epsilon(z)<\theta$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(a_\epsilon,\infty)$ and $U_\epsilon(z)>\theta$ on $(0,a_\epsilon)$. Moreover, as $\epsilon\to0$, one has $c_\epsilon\to c_f$ and $a_\epsilon\to+\infty$. If $\mathcal S_\epsilon=\{(U_\epsilon(z),Q_\epsilon(z)):\, z\in\mathbb R\}$ denotes the associated homoclinic orbit, then $d_H(\mathcal S_\epsilon,\mathcal S_0)=0$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, i.e. $\mathcal S_\epsilon=\mathcal S_0$ as subsets of $(U,Q)$-space.

ALS.justification: The stem asks for the “strongest statement asserting existence together with uniqueness … and ε→0 limit behavior,” which strongly cues that the correct option will be the most comprehensive theorem-like package (existence+uniqueness+parameter curves+limit+Hausdorff convergence). This is not an explicit giveaway, but it narrows the target to the longest/most detailed option.

TAS.justification: The item is essentially a theorem-selection question: it asks for the strongest correct existence/uniqueness/limit statement under the stated assumptions, rather than requiring derivation. There is some nontrivial discrimination among variants (e.g., aε→∞ vs finite, exact equality of orbits, quantitative rates), but it still largely restates a result.

GPS.justification: To choose correctly, one must compare subtle asymptotic/uniqueness claims (e.g., divergence of pulse width, nature of convergence, uniqueness of parameter curves). However, because the choices are near-copies differing by small phrases, the task is more about recognizing the right theorem-strength than generating/deriving reasoning from the system.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common over/under-claiming failure modes: (B) wrong limit for aε, (C) weaker but potentially true statement, (D) unjustified quantitative rate, (E) impossible exact identification Sε=S0. They are distinct, aligned with typical errors, and not obviously absurd.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: A solid theorem-strength discrimination MCQ with good, realistic distractors. Main weakness is mild answer-leakage via the stem’s “strongest statement” framing and the fact that it functions more as theorem recognition than a problem that forces substantive derivation from the model.

theorem.content:
\label{thmd}
The optimal Jordan constant for the volume-preserving plane Cremona group $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2, \Delta)$ is $12$.
theorem.label: thmd

sketch: To find the Jordan constant in Theorem~\ref{thmd}, the paper outlines the following strategy: in Section~2 it reviews preliminaries on finite subgroups of $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2)$ and volume-preserving maps; in Section~3 it ``derive[s] the exact sequence as above, which reduces the task of finding a Jordan constant to enumerating certain Calabi-Yau pairs on $G$-minimal surfaces''; in Section~4 it ``explicitly find[s] the Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2, \Delta)$''; and in Section~5 it shows ``that this Jordan constant is optimal'' and gives ``a way to find volume-preserving subgroups regularized on del Pezzo surfaces.''
expanded_sketch: To find the Jordan constant in the main theorem, the paper outlines the following strategy: next it reviews preliminaries on finite subgroups of $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2)$ and volume-preserving maps; then it ``derive[s] the exact sequence as above, which reduces the task of finding a Jordan constant to enumerating certain Calabi-Yau pairs on $G$-minimal surfaces''; next it ``explicitly find[s] the Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2, \Delta)$''; and finally it shows ``that this Jordan constant is optimal'' and gives ``a way to find volume-preserving subgroups regularized on del Pezzo surfaces.''
expanded_theorem:
\label{thmd}
The optimal Jordan constant for the volume-preserving plane Cremona group $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2, \Delta)$ is $12$.

mcq.question: Let $G=\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$ be the volume-preserving plane Cremona group. Recall that a Jordan constant for $G$ is an integer $J$ such that every finite subgroup of $G$ contains an abelian normal subgroup of index at most $J$, and the optimal Jordan constant is the smallest such $J$. What is the strongest statement asserting existence and uniqueness of the optimal Jordan constant for $G$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists a unique optimal (i.e. minimal) Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$, and this optimal Jordan constant equals $12$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists a (not necessarily unique) optimal Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$, and the optimal Jordan constant is at most $12$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists a Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$, and one may take $J=12$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists a unique optimal Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$, and this optimal Jordan constant equals $60$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: There exists a unique optimal Jordan constant for $\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$, and for every finite subgroup $F\le \mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2,\Delta)$ there is an abelian subgroup $A\le F$ (not assumed normal) of index at most $12$.

sketch_usage_meta.label: C
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: drops optimality/uniqueness; keeps existence with explicit bound

sketch_usage_meta.label: D
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: replaces enumerated optimal constant $12$ by classical Cremona bound $60$

sketch_usage_meta.label: E
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: replaces 'abelian normal subgroup' by 'abelian subgroup' while keeping index bound $12$

ALS.justification: The stem effectively telegraphs the intended answer by asking for the “strongest statement” about existence/uniqueness and then offering an option that asserts uniqueness/minimality and a specific value (12). The presence of a clearly weaker-true option (“one may take J=12”) also points toward the stronger version with the same number.

TAS.justification: The question is essentially a restatement/comparison of definitions (“optimal = smallest”) plus a memorized fact (the value 12). It does not set up a scenario requiring application; it mainly asks which phrasing is strongest.

GPS.justification: Little to no generative reasoning is needed beyond recognizing that ‘unique optimal constant’ is tautologically true once existence is known, and recalling/spotting the correct numeric constant. The task is primarily selecting the most assertive wording rather than deriving anything.

DQS.justification: Distractors reflect common failure modes (confusing normal vs not-necessarily-normal; mixing up 12 vs 60; weakening to an upper bound; dropping optimality). However, option B is awkward (“optimal constant … at most 12” contradicts ‘optimal/minimal’ phrasing), and overall the set makes A stand out as the only fully coherent ‘strongest’ formulation.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: Low-quality as a reasoning-assessment item: it largely tests recall/recognition of the claimed Jordan constant and the ability to pick the most strongly worded statement, with noticeable answer leakage and limited genuine mathematical reasoning. Distractors are somewhat aligned to typical confusions but not uniformly well-formed.

theorem.content:
(\cite[conjecture~1.20]{KaKuMGSt})
\label{conj1}
$\xi_{g,1}$ is the unique closed, embedded minimal surface $M$ of genus $g\geq 2$ in $\mathbb{S}^3$ whose isometry group contains a Klein subgroup $\Z_2\times \Z_2=\langle \phi,\phi'\rangle$ such that $\phi,\phi'$ are reflections across orthogonal spheres $S,S'\subset \mathbb{S}^3$ (orientation-reversing on $M$), the closures $\Omega^+,\Omega^-=\phi(\Omega^+)$ of the components of $M\setminus S$
have genus zero, and all the boundary components of $\partial \Omega^+=\partial \Omega^-$ intersect the great circle $S\cap S'$.
theorem.label: conj1

post_theorem_intro_text:
It is worth mentioning a recent work by Kusner, L\"{u} and Wang~\cite{kuluwa1} where they characterize the Lawson surface $\xi_{m,k}$ among closed embedded surfaces of genus $mk$ in $\mathbb{S}^3$ that minimize the Willmore functional and are invariant under any group conjugate
to the maximal rotation-symmetry group within Iso$(\xi_{m,k})$. As a consequence, the same authors prove (Theorem~4.2 in~\cite{kuluwa1})
a similar characterization for $\xi_{m,k}$ as the one by Kapouleas and 
Wiygul~\cite{KaWiy0} among closed embedded minimal surfaces of genus $mk$ in $\mathbb{S}^3$ which are invariant under certain index-two subroups of Iso$(\xi_{m,k})$. 

We will prove a result closely related to Conjecture~\ref{conj1} in the case of genus $g=2$, strengthening the assumption on the Klein subgroup of $O_{48}$ by the product $D_{4h}=\Z_2\times D_4$ of $\Z_2$ (generated by a reflection $\phi$ across a sphere $S\subset \mathbb{S}^3$ so that $S$ disconnects $M$ into two genus zero components) with the dihedral group $D_4$ of order 8, see Theorem~\ref{mainthm} for a precise statement. For this reason, surfaces invariant by $\Z_2\times D_4$ are called $D_{4h}$-symmetric. Our assumption on $D_{4h}$-symmetry in Theorem~\ref{mainthm} allows to drop the hypothesis of Conjecture~\ref{conj1} on all boundary components of $\partial \Omega_1^+=\partial \Omega_1^-$ intersecting a great circle of $S$.

In order to prove Theorem~\ref{mainthm}, we first describe 
the fundamental piece of an embedded, $D_{4h}$-symmetric minimal surface of genus two, and show that under conjugation, an appropriate reflection of 
this conjugate fundamental piece is bounded by a geodesic pentagon in $\mathbb{S}^3$ with right angles at all its vertices. We then study the space of such geodesic, right-angled polygons, which is a two-parameter family $\mathcal P_{l, \omega}$, $(l, \omega) \in [(0, \pi)\times (-\pi/2,\pi/2)]\setminus \{ (\pi/2,0)\}$, and related one-parameter family $\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}$,
$\sigma \in [0,\pi/2]$ that describes the parameter choice $(l,\omega)=
(\pi/2,0)$ for the first family. We next show that these pentagons are the boundary of (embedded) area-minimizing disks $\Sigma _{l , \omega}$ (resp.
$\Sigma_{\sigma}$), and explore the geometric properties of $\Sigma _{l, \omega},\Sigma_\sigma$. Among these properties, we are particularly interested in understanding the behavior of the mapping that associates to each $(l, \omega)$ (resp. $\sigma$) the length $L$ of a reflective geodesic $\g_{l,\omega}\subset 
\S_{l,\omega}$ (resp. $\g_{\sigma}\subset \S_{\sigma}$). The level set 
$L=\pi/2$ of this function consists of the only potential examples that after conjugation and Schwarz reflection, might give rise to fundamental pieces of our desired $D_{4h}$-minimal surfaces of genus two. We then analyze the closing problem
for the surfaces arising in the level set $L=\pi/2$, in the sense of
determining under which conditions the conjugate piece $\Sigma_{l,\omega}^*$ of $\Sigma_{l,\omega}$ with $L=\pi/2$, produces after Schwarz 
reflection an embedded, $D_{4h}$-symmetric minimal surface. We will prove that this closing problem has a unique solution, from which we will deduce the desired uniqueness result. See Section~\ref{sec2.6} for a detailed 
description of the distribution of the paper.

(2) They "study the space of such geodesic, right-angled polygons," a two-parameter family $\mathcal P_{l, \omega}$ with $(l,\omega)\in[(0,\pi)\times(-\pi/2,\pi/2)]\setminus\{(\pi/2,0)\}$, and a related one-parameter family $\mathcal P_\sigma$, $\sigma\in[0,\pi/2]$, corresponding to the excluded parameter choice $(l,\omega)=(\pi/2,0)$. \label{conj1}

mcq.question: Fix an integer genus \(g\ge 2\). Consider closed, embedded minimal surfaces \(M\subset \mathbb S^3\) of genus \(g\) whose isometry group contains a Klein four subgroup \(\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2=\langle\phi,\phi'\rangle\) such that \(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) are reflections across orthogonal 2-spheres \(S,S'\subset\mathbb S^3\) (and are orientation-reversing on \(M\)); if \(\Omega^+\) and \(\Omega^-:=\phi(\Omega^+)\) denote the closures of the components of \(M\setminus S\), then \(\Omega^+\) and \(\Omega^-\) have genus zero; and every boundary component of \(\partial\Omega^+=\partial\Omega^-\) intersects the great circle \(S\cap S'\). Under these conditions, which existence-and-uniqueness statement is asserted?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists exactly one closed, embedded minimal surface \(M\subset\mathbb S^3\) of genus \(g\ge 2\) satisfying all of the stated symmetry and topological conditions, and this unique surface is \(\xi_{g,1}\).

choices.label: B
choices.text: For each integer genus $g\ge 2$, there exists at least one closed, embedded minimal surface $M\subset\mathbb S^3$ satisfying the stated Klein-four symmetry, the genus--zero condition on $\Omega^\pm$, and the requirement that every component of $\partial\Omega^+=\partial\Omega^-$ meets the great circle $S\cap S'$, and any two such surfaces are congruent up to an ambient isometry of $\mathbb S^3$ that preserves $S\cap S'$ setwise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For each integer genus $g\ge 2$, there exists at most one closed, embedded minimal surface $M\subset\mathbb S^3$ satisfying the stated Klein-four symmetry, the genus--zero condition on $\Omega^\pm$, and the requirement that every component of $\partial\Omega^+=\partial\Omega^-$ meets the great circle $S\cap S'$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For each integer genus $g\ge 2$, there exists exactly one closed, embedded minimal surface $M\subset\mathbb S^3$ satisfying the stated conditions, and moreover the isometry group of this $M$ contains a dihedral subgroup $D_{4h}$ generated by reflections in $S$ and $S'$ together with a half--turn about the great circle $S\cap S'$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For each integer genus $g\ge 2$, there exists exactly one closed, embedded minimal surface $M\subset\mathbb S^3$ satisfying the stated conditions, and this $M$ is characterized by the fact that in the associated two--parameter family of right--angled geodesic pentagons $\mathcal P_{l,\omega}$ one has a unique parameter pair $(l,\omega)\in(0,\pi)\times(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ producing a reflective geodesic $\gamma_{l,\omega}$ of length $L=\pi/2$.

ALS.justification: The correct option A essentially restates the stem’s setup as an 'existence-and-uniqueness statement' and names the purported unique surface \(\xi_{g,1}\). theorem.label: def:ubq

post_theorem_intro_text:
The property (\ref{eq:BQ}){} is easily checked to be a quasi-isometry invariant among geodesic spaces. 
Thus, it makes sense to say that a finitely generated group has this property. The Euclidean and hyperbolic planes obviously have (\ref{eq:BQ}){}, by the Jordan curve theorem. It is an exercise in hyperbolic geometry to show that if an infinite hyperbolic group satisfies (\ref{eq:BQ}){} then its Gromov boundary is circular. Hence, the convergence group theorem implies the following.

\begin{theorem*}[Corollary of the convergence group theorem]
    Let $G$ be an infinite hyperbolic group with (\ref{eq:BQ}){}. Then $G$ is virtually Fuchsian.
\end{theorem*}

In this form, the hypotheses now make sense in any finitely generated group, or indeed in any locally finite, quasi-transitive graph.
It is therefore natural to ask whether this theorem extends to non-hyperbolic groups or to arbitrary locally finite, quasi-transitive graphs. This question appears as Problem~14.98 of the Kourovka Notebook \cite{khukhro2025unsolvedproblemsgrouptheory}, posed by V. A. Churkin in 1999. 
In this paper, we answer Churkin's question in the affirmative and prove the following.

\begin{restatable}{alphtheorem}{main}\label{thm:main-theorem}
    Let $X$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive graph with (\ref{eq:BQ}){}. Then $X$ is quasi-isometric to either the Euclidean plane or the hyperbolic plane.  
\end{restatable}

Since finitely generated abelian groups and Fuchsian groups are known to be quasi-isometrically rigid, this has the consequence that if $G$ is a finitely generated group with (\ref{eq:BQ}){} then $G$ is a virtual surface group. Thus we provide a new, purely geometric characterisation of virtual surface groups among all finitely generated groups.

We remark that Theorem~\ref{thm:main-theorem} can be compared to Bing's characterisation of the 2-sphere \cite{bing1946kline}. This states that any compact, connected, locally connected space without cut-points or cut-pairs, in which every simple closed curve separates, is homeomorphic to the 2-sphere. Morally, our theorem is a coarse analogue of this statement for locally finite, quasi-transitive graphs.
We also point out that our characterisation is similar in spirit to Papasoglu's theorem mentioned above, in the sense that they both characterise virtual surface groups through the separation properties of their quasi-lines. One key difference between the two results is that Papasoglu requires the group to be \emph{a priori} finitely presented, whereas we do away with this assumption altogether.

\subsection*{Outline}

Before we begin, we describe a rough outline of this paper and the proof therein.
In order to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:main-theorem}, we consider separately the cases where $X$ is hyperbolic and where $X$ is not hyperbolic. The hyperbolic case follows from the convergence group theorem as discussed above.\footnote{The case where $X$ is hyperbolic but not a Cayley graph requires some care, but still follows from known results; see~\cite[\S1.1]{macmanus2024note}.} Our attention is thus entirely focused on the case where $X$ is not hyperbolic.
The ultimate goal is to prove that non-hyperbolicity plus (\ref{eq:BQ}){} implies that $X$ has quadratic growth. From here, a theorem of Trofimov  \cite{trofimov1985graphs}, building on work of Gromov \cite{gromov1981groups}, plus the Bass--Guivarc'h formula for the degrees of growth of nilpotent groups \cite{bass1972degree, guivarc1973croissance}, allows us to conclude that $X$ is quasi-isometric to the Euclidean plane.

We will study this problem through the eyes of \emph{witnesses}, which are introduced in \S\ref{sec:witness}. These are pairs of rays which probe deep into the two wide components bound by a bi-infinite quasi-geodesic. A key tool here will be the \emph{witness protection lemma}, which asserts that if we perturb a bi-infinite geodesic in a bounded way, then the original witnesses still witness two distinct deep components bound by the new quasi-geodesic. Following this, in \S\ref{sec:crosshair} and \S\ref{sec:witness-sep} we construct and consider a large figure called a \emph{cross-examiner}. Attaching paths to the cross-examiner and applying the witness protection lemma allows us to construct closed loops which coarsely bound regions of $X$ in a controlled way. These loops should be compared to Jordan curves in the plane. Combining this with an inequality of Varopoulos, 
in \S\ref{sec:jurisdiction} we establish a useful criterion for showing that $X$ has quadratic growth. 

Following this, we study the separation properties of \emph{quasi-circles} and, more generally, \emph{truncated quasi-circles} in \S\ref{sec:circles}. We apply our new criterion for quadratic growth and see that either  all (truncated) quasi-circles coarsely bound regions of at most uniformly bounded depth, regardless of length, or $X$ has quadratic growth. In the language of this paper, we prove that truncated quasi-circles have \emph{limited jurisdiction}. In the final section, \S\ref{sec:final}, we apply the Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem to construct a sequence of `nested' truncated quasi-circles lying along a bi-infinite quasi-geodesic. We then observe that this `nesting' taken together with the witness protection lemma means the truncated quasi-circles cannot possibly have limited jurisdiction. This enables us to conclude that $X$ has quadratic growth, and deliver our final verdict.

\subsection*{Acknowledgements}

 I thank Panos Papasoglu for helpful discussions about bigons, and Agelos Georgakopoulos for comments. This work was supported by the Heilbronn Institute for Mathematical Research.

mcq.question: Let $X$ be a geodesic metric space. Call a connected subspace $Z\subset X$ **narrow** if (with the ambient metric) it is quasi-isometric to a subset of $\mathbf{R}$, and **wide** otherwise. Under these definitions, what is the precise existence-and-uniqueness statement (in terms of the number of wide connected components) expressing that $X$ has the uniformly bisecting quasi-geodesics property (UBQ)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists $\sigma>0$ such that for every connected, bi-infinite quasi-geodesic $\rho\subset X$, the complement $X\setminus N_\sigma(\rho)$ contains exactly two wide connected components.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists $\sigma>0$ such that for every connected, bi-infinite quasi-geodesic $\rho\subset X$, the complement $X\setminus N_\sigma(\rho)$ contains at least two wide connected components.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every connected, bi-infinite quasi-geodesic $\rho\subset X$, there exists $\sigma>0$ such that $X\setminus N_\sigma(\rho)$ contains exactly two wide connected components.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists $\sigma>0$ such that for every connected, bi-infinite quasi-geodesic $\rho\subset X$, the complement $X\setminus N_\sigma(\rho)$ contains exactly two connected components, and both of these components are wide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: There exists $\sigma>0$ such that for every connected, bi-infinite quasi-geodesic $\rho\subset X$, the complement $X\setminus N_\sigma(\rho)$ contains exactly two connected components, each of which is wide.

ALS.justification: The stem does not state the answer or give a direct hint like “exactly two wide components”; it asks for the precise quantifier/uniqueness formulation, which must be inferred from the options.

TAS.justification: It is essentially a “state the definition precisely” item: it asks for the exact existence-and-uniqueness statement that *is* the UBQ property, rather than applying UBQ to a new situation.

GPS.justification: Selecting the correct choice requires some reasoning about subtle differences (uniform vs. non-uniform σ; 'exactly two' vs 'at least two'; wide components vs all components), but for anyone who knows UBQ it is largely recall/recognition.

DQS.justification: Most distractors target realistic failure modes (wrong quantifier order; weakening 'exactly' to 'at least'; confusing wide components with total connected components). However D and E are effectively duplicates, reducing distinctiveness and overall distractor quality.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: A mostly definition-recall MCQ with decent quantifier-based distractors; it avoids answer leakage but is tautological and has some distractor redundancy (D/E).
